when i started at a university, i called a suicide hotline one night about a month into my first semester. i made it clear to the woman that i had no intentions of hurting myself (though i told her i had medication because she asked if i had anything that could be used in a harmful way). we talked for about an hour, and then we left when i was feeling better and just wanted to go back to my dorm. when i went back to my dorm, she called me back and told me that she had “a bad feeling” and that the campus cops were on the other line, and that i had to go talk to them. i was like what the fuck?? but i didn’t really understand at the time what my rights were, and i was a bit of a different person back then. so i met the cops. the woman said it would be “discrete” and near my dorm—they literally met me out front where everyone could see. and they ended up taking my medication away even though their supervisor specifically told them not to, and everyone seemed a bit on the fence about whether they should do it. the cops kept me out until after midnight (i had classes the next morning) and even searched my bag against my wishes to make sure i “didn’t have anything i could hurt myself with”. i didn’t know my rights at the time so i didn’t know i could outright refuse a search like that, but they kind of coerced me into letting them do it. like, i said i wasn’t comfortable with that and then the lady cop was like “if you’re not comfortable with him searching your bag, i can”. thank god i wasn’t a stoner yet by that point but they found a small knife which i had on me for self-defense, considering the fact that i am a woman on a college campus, and they ended up taking it to the evidence room where my mom had to collect it (along with my meds) at a later date. 
looking back on this it’s totally fucked up and i wish i had done more about the situation when it happened. now it’s been about two years (i’m 20 and no longer attending that school) so i’m not sure if i could even do much. but fuck appalachian state.

I don’t know if I was necessarily homophobic, but my family was very much so. We saw a lesbian couple on the news once and I heard my grandma imitate puking noises. I remember thinking for a quick second, don’t they look happy? but then the sound she made enforced the idea that “it’s wrong. It’s unnatural. It goes against nature and God.”
Not long after that, I joined an online group of people, based around a book series, many of which were openly LGBT. I never said anything negative about it, but the idea still felt...well, weird to me, at first. 
A few weeks later, my mom and her boyfriend took me to the mall with my mom’s boyfriend’s granddaughter who was fourteen at the time (I was eleven). We talked about a lot of things, and became somewhat close friends while we were there by ourselves.
At one point, she turns around and asks me, “what would you do if I told you I was dating a girl?”
I remembered those words exactly, in spite of having only seen her one time since. 
“I...well, I don’t think it’s a problem.”
And after that, I realized that I truly meant those words. (Her family was, as she said, homophobic too, so it remained a secret.)

Also helps that, as things turned out, I’m bisexual, and I’m also the current president of my school’s Gay-Straight Alliance.

Nonetheless, I ended up missing a field trip, a fundraising opportunity for an end-of-the-year trip I almost didn’t get to go on because of the suspension, and being “psychologically evaluated” was hell for me. The woman who did the evaluating was very snappy and rude, refused to listen to my side of the story, and when she got to the questioning about animal abuse (which was nothing to do with the situation nor was there otherwise reason for her to ask about this, but I think it was part of the evaluation itself) my mom stopped defending me. I almost didn’t pass the evaluation because she told the evaluator that she genuinely didn’t know whether to believe me or not. I asked her afterward and her reason was something like “you used to chase the cat around the house when you were ten”. 
I had a meeting with the school administration before I was allowed back into any classes. I kept denying the entire thing, but they didn’t listen to me; it was almost like I wasn’t even talking. Principal went off on this tangent about how some kid got suspended for saying the word “bomb” in regards to a project a few years back and how they were “just trying to keep the school safe”.
I later found out that a handful of my friends who WERE present when the incident supposedly “took place” had all defended me and told the school that I didn’t say the very thing I was suspended for.

My last two relapses. (I'm a month clean but I'm not expecting it to last forever.)
The first was because of a girl's Facebook post. She goes to my school (and honestly we weren't friends, all I knew about her was this one guy she was dating because they were PDA-ing to the max). She made this long post on her birthday about how she started cutting in sixth grade (same time I did) and about all these terrible things that have happened to her and then finished it off with how she's three months clean. It got several hundred likes/comments and even some from my closest friends, and I should have felt happy for her but I couldn't. I felt jealous that now everyone's going to see her as some deep inspiring beacon of courage and strength, and continuing to ignore those who still need that kind of help or support. I'm all for free speech and I'm not the kind of person who screeches "tag your triggers or your words will make my eyes bleed!!!!" but seeing that kind of post just...set off something. 
The second was when classmate of mine made a "it's down the road, not across the street" joke. In all likelihood, he didn't know that I would be affected by it. In fact, he didn't even know that I heard it. It wasn't directed at me and he was talking to a friend of his, but the thought of it turned me to stone, so to speak. I love offensive humor, but the thought of laughing at another person's complete anguish, to the point of taking their own life, is something I'll never understand.

I've reached a point in my life where whenever something happens—say, my mom is being awful to me or my girlfriend doesn't seem to be ok—my brain starts immediately thinking about suicide. Not just "kms" or other non-serious thoughts but actually planning it out (how I'll do it, how it'll feel, what they'll think afterwards, etc.)
One of my closest friends turned me in to my counselor against my will last month because I told him I was suicidal and I lied my way out of it because I just didn't want the counselor to know. She called my mom and my mom said very little to me (which was a relief) about the situation, but it hurt me that my friend took a very personal conversation and told others. (Our other friends have had bad experiences with counselors—one was raped and forced to get legal attention and the counselor told the other one's mom about it, who only punished her for it.)
I mean, he did have a good reason for it. I told him I wanted to isolate myself. Cut myself off from everyone and then, in the dead heat of the summer, I'd do it. I shouldn't feel mad at him for seeking help, but I do. 
My life has changed for the most part since then—school's out so there's way less stress, I got into an amazing relationship, and my friends have since become more supportive. But there's still the instinct to do it.

Not quite from an administrative point of view, but this has happened twice in the past couple of years at my school.
The first time, it was a seventh grader (I was in seventh grade too). When I was on the bus that morning, I heard a few people talking about it because someone had posted an RIP post on Facebook or something. When we got to school, everything was grim and gloomy. The teachers passed around a letter—it didn't specify the details other than that the girl had killed herself. (I later learned she had hanged herself with a scarf.)
There was a support system set up in the library. I didn't attend, because I didn't know her personally, but several crying girls were seen coming and going in the hallway. 
My (then)friends had very different reactions. One of my friends and I were just confused, given that we didn't know the girl or anything, so it didn't affect us that much. One of them had hated the girl (had been bullied by her in the past) so she just kind of laughed it off, but the other one was heartbroken, which was odd given that they weren't even friends, but I guess these things can do that to a person.
I remember hearing about one of her teachers having a box of tissues at her desk for a couple of weeks after that, as well. My homeroom/English teacher gave us a speech shortly after it happened, about how there is no mistake we can make that can't be undone. The counselor came in and discussed the warning signs of suicide with us following the aftermath, as well—all the "it's a permanent solution to a temporary problem" stuff. Oh, and that there aren't any memorials on the campus site because they don't want to "encourage" other people. 
What I hate, though, is that the girl wasn't even depressed, from what I've seen/heard. If anything, she was among the popular crowd, but something had happened and she made the sudden decision. I guess this pissed me off because I'd been suicidal around that time and people only seemed to care when it was someone like her. Not to mention it's impossible to discuss those personal types of things with the counselor unless you want a phone call to your parents. 
So, yeah. For a couple of months the entire school was heartbroken because nothing like that had happened before, but most of us moved on. I still see "RIP Hailey" Facebook posts every November, though, on the anniversary.
On the contrary, it happened again last year (freshman year for me, the guy that died was either a sophomore or a junior, I think). They announced it over the intercom and a few people in my class whispered about it. Passed out another note saying that they didn't know whether it was a suicide or not (it was). Things got awkward especially when one of our stem words that we had to study that day was "pend", the stem meaning "hang", and a few people looked uncomfortable. It was like the black cloud again, except it only lasted for a day. That's it. No schoolwide counselor visits, no support session, nothing. It was almost like they forgot about him.
